label: Chapter Question
notes: Open by putting Chapter 3 in contrast with the earlier curve chapters. In the plane, a curve has a preferred normal direction, a signed scalar curvature, a signed area functional, and a tangent map into the unit circle. Those extra structures turn local bending into global integers and variational equations.

label: Lecture Route
notes: Use this route slide as the contract for the lecture. Every topic has a visual object and a checkable quantity: curvature should agree with angle change, sector area should track orientation, elastica should reduce to an equation for kappa, and regular homotopy should preserve tangent winding when closedness is required.

label: J Operator
notes: Before defining curvature, slow down on the operator J. It is not decoration; it is the reason plane curves have signed curvature instead of only a curvature magnitude. The determinant identity tells students that rotating the first vector by ninety degrees converts orientation into an inner product.

label: Signed Curvature
notes: The main teaching point is that the sign of kappa is a comparison between the actual change in tangent and the positive normal J T. A left turn has one sign and a right turn has the other. The determinant formula then gives a parametrization-independent way to compute the same signed quantity.

label: Reconstruction
notes: Here the curvature function becomes a construction recipe rather than just a measurement. Integrate kappa to obtain the tangent angle, turn that angle into a unit tangent, and integrate once more to get the curve. Congruence freedom remains because the initial point and initial direction were choices.

label: Sector Area
notes: Emphasize that sector area is signed swept area, not simply the visible bounded region. The origin ray can sweep the same region more than once, and clockwise pieces subtract. This makes the formula powerful for variations but dangerous if students read it as ordinary unsigned area.

label: Area Variation
notes: This slide ties sector area back to variational calculus from Chapter 2. For compactly supported variations, the derivative of area pairs the variational field with J gamma prime. When length is constrained by fixed sector area, the Euler-Lagrange condition forces constant curvature, so the critical images are lines or circles.

label: Planar Elastica
notes: The reduction to a scalar ODE is the reward for working in the plane. Total squared curvature becomes one half the integral of kappa squared, and the elastic equation is now an equation for kappa alone. The potential picture helps students remember which curvature values are dynamically allowed.

label: Area-Constrained Elastica
notes: The extra sector-area constraint adds a constant forcing term to the elastica equation. Interpret mu as the term that keeps the signed area from drifting while the curve tries to lower bending energy. This is where length, area, and bending energy become a coupled variational system.

label: Total Curvature
notes: Total curvature is the integral form of angle change. For a closed curve, the tangent returns to its starting direction, so the lifted tangent angle can only change by an integer multiple of two pi. That integer is the first global invariant in the course.

label: Winding Gallery
notes: Use the gallery to separate the curve in the plane from the path traced by its tangent on the unit circle. A curve can self-intersect, bend back, or be traversed in different ways, but the tangent winding records the net number of turns made by the tangent direction.

label: Open Regular Homotopy
notes: For open plane curves, regular homotopy is flexible. The proof strategy normalizes length, arclength parametrization, starting point, and starting tangent, then interpolates curvature functions and reconstructs curves. The keyword regular means the velocity never vanishes during the deformation.

label: Closed Classification
notes: Closed curves introduce a real obstruction. During a closed regular homotopy, the winding number is both continuous in the homotopy parameter and integer valued, so it cannot jump. Whitney-Graustein says this obstruction is complete: equal winding is exactly the condition for closed regular homotopy.

label: Closure Repair
notes: The proof of the closed classification has a subtle repair step. Curvature interpolation gives a regular path of curves, but the intermediate curves may fail to close. Subtracting the average tangent drift closes the curve, and the key estimate proves that the modified velocity is still nonzero.

label: Notebook Checks
notes: This is the computational audit station. The notebook does not ask students to trust the pictures; it records numerical witnesses. The circle area error, winding error, and speed check are small because the sampled construction preserves the intended identities within tolerance.

label: Pitfalls
notes: These are the mistakes to call out before the lecture ends. Sign conventions depend on the chosen positive rotation, sector area depends on the origin unless the setup cancels that dependence, and ordinary homotopy is weaker than regular homotopy because it allows the derivative to vanish.

label: Summary
notes: Close by linking the chapter's local and global ideas. Signed curvature is the local signal, sector area and bending energy are functionals built from the curve, planar elastica turns variation into an ODE, and tangent winding is the global integer that classifies closed regular homotopy classes.
